lesson_title: Two Valleys, One Ridge: How Every Reaction Pays Its Way
hook_text: A gas stove leaks energy-rich fuel past a flame-hot element — and nothing happens until the spark. Why?
clip_script: If burning wood is such a generous payout, here is the awkward question: why is any tree still standing? Why does your braai sit inert — wood touching oxygen all afternoon — until someone finally strikes a match? Because even the most generous reaction charges admission. The old bonds must be winched open BEFORE the new bonds can drop and pay, and that winching bill lands first. Think of a business with guaranteed profit that still needs startup capital: no capital, no doors open, no profit — ever. That startup demand is the activation energy. The match is a startup loan. It lifts a few molecules over the admission price; their reaction pays out; the payout covers admission for the molecules beside them; and from that moment the fire is self-financing. One match, a whole evening of coals. And a catalyst? A tunnel through the ridge — the crossing gets cheaper and faster, but the valleys never move, so the payout never changes.
visual_style: A stubborn unlit braai at golden hour; one match flare triggering a chain of glowing molecule crossings; cut to a clean side-profile mountain with two valleys, a ridge, and a dashed tunnel punching through.
mood: Everyday mystery, cleanly solved — curiosity flipping into confidence.
pacing: Cold-open question, slow beat on the untouched wood, accelerating chain-reaction montage, calm tunnel epilogue.
